lesson.title: Bandwidth: Measuring the Gap Between Two Cutoffs
lesson.summary: Bandwidth is the width, in frequency, of a filter's passband between its two half power points, the number that ties cutoff frequency, passband, and stopband together.
lesson.body:
Bandwidth ties together the last three ideas into one number. It is defined as the width, in frequency, of a filter's passband, measured between its cutoff frequencies. For a filter with two edges, an upper cutoff f_H and a lower cutoff f_L, bandwidth is simply BW equals f_H minus f_L. Everything inside that width is passband; everything outside it is stopband.

The clearest place to see this is a series RLC circuit built to pass a band of frequencies around its resonance. Take R equals 100 ohms, L equals 1 H, and C equals 1 microfarad, that is 1 times 10 to the negative 6 farads. The center, or resonant, angular frequency is omega_0 equals 1 over the square root of LC. Here LC equals 1 times 1 times 10 to the negative 6, which is 1 times 10 to the negative 6, and its square root is 1 times 10 to the negative 3. So omega_0 equals 1 divided by (1 times 10 to the negative 3), which is 1000 rad/s.

The two half power frequencies of a series RLC bandpass response are given by omega equals plus or minus R over 2L, added to the square root of (R over 2L) squared plus omega_0 squared. Here R over 2L equals 100 over 2, which is 50. Squaring gives 2500. Adding omega_0 squared, which is 1000 squared, or 1,000,000, gives 1,002,500. Its square root is approximately 1001.249. So the upper half power frequency is omega_2 equals 50 plus 1001.249, which is 1051.249 rad/s, and the lower one is omega_1 equals negative 50 plus 1001.249, which is 951.249 rad/s.

The bandwidth in rad/s is omega_2 minus omega_1, which is 1051.249 minus 951.249, exactly 100 rad/s, regardless of any rounding in the square root step, since the 1001.249 term cancels out of the subtraction. Notice that this equals R over L directly, since 100 over 1 is also 100, a shortcut worth remembering: for a series RLC circuit, bandwidth in rad/s always equals R divided by L, no square roots required. Converting to Hz, f_1 equals 951.249 over 2 pi, which is about 151.4 Hz, and f_2 equals 1051.249 over 2 pi, which is about 167.3 Hz, giving a bandwidth of f_2 minus f_1 equals about 15.9 Hz, matching R over (2 pi L), which is 100 over 6.2832, also about 15.9 Hz.

So this circuit passes frequencies from about 151.4 Hz to about 167.3 Hz with little loss, that stretch is its passband, everything outside it is stopband, and the roughly 15.9 Hz gap between the two cutoff frequencies is its bandwidth. This exact circuit, with the same R, L, and C, reappears later in this unit when quality factor and resonance are introduced, since bandwidth is one of the two numbers, along with resonant frequency, that quality factor is built from.
